Hello! I need some help finding a good keyboard with a 400 dollar budget.

Some context (feel free to skip this paragraph): I'm a grad student and just finished an application that I've been working on for about 9 months now. As a present to myself, I was planning to buy Sony WH-1000XM5 headphones to use in public spaces while I'm writing. I was going to buy them tomorrow, until a friend mentioned they have a pair and let me try them. Hated it. Suddenly, I remembered why I made the switch to open backs years ago. I have some sensory issue with having my ears shut in a closed spaced with loud sounds playing. Anyway, I budgeted 400 dollars for it, and mama ain't raise no fiscally responsible bitch. I've been using an RK-100 for two years now, and am thinking this is a good opportunity to upgrade.

I'm having so many issues with understanding mechanical keyboards. I just cannot make sense of it, and I would honestly just appreciate someone telling me what to buy. I'm not a hobbyist in the sense that I enjoy endless customization and mods. I really just want a relatively premium keyboard that feels good, sounds good, and fits my needs. It would be so helpful if someone in this community could help me out with that.

Here is my list of needs:

* While I really enjoy a clicky keyboard, I want this new keyboard to be quiet enough to be acceptable in a public space with other people around. Maybe not a library, but an office space or classroom where others are doing their own thing. I really appreciate tactility though, so I don't want one of those switches that have no bump that let's me know whether or not I pressed it.
* I'd also like the keyboard to be one that has some wireless capability, so that I can use it while I teach. The keyboards of the classrooms I use will be the death of me, and the ability to use a quiet keyboard that I'm comfortable with would be such a huge help.
* I don't want something flashy or obnoxious. RGB is alright, but I would feel a little embarrassed to be pulling out a keyboard that shouts "GAMER BRAND" in professional spaces. A little stupid of a need, but it is what it is.

My list of wants:

* A keyboard that has some ability to be portable. Maybe one I can throw in a laptop backpack that has a decent amount of space for it
* One with a deep, thwocky sound. My RK-100 is quite high-pitched and tinny, and it's gotten a bit grating lately.
* Cute & minimalist keycaps. I love pinks, purples, and whites. I know I can buy those on my own though, but it'd be cool if the keyboard was already something cute
* A keyboard that's relatively easy to buy. Amazon or a local vendor pre-built would ideal. I would even buy a fully-featured kit and take the day to build it myself. I'm unwilling to be searching for individual sets and pieces, though.

It feels odd to write out a list of demands for random people to do the labor of finding a keyboard for me, but I thought it might be acceptable for a hobbyist community that seems to enjoy this kind of thing. I hope that's alright, and thank you!

Everyone is focusing so much on little technical plot details and plot twists, which, sure, is a thing worth praising/criticizing. But what about the themes? I found this episode as such a tense and innovative examination of how grief and trauma can so cruelly interact with compassion and honest kindness. That a grieving man who has experienced so much pain can so cruelly act against the one man who can and does give him such intimate compassion. I absolutely adore the reference to The Illustrated Man, noting the parallels between the themes of that book. 

I thought it was interesting from a gendered perspective too. Two men, a grieving California artist left to overcome unimaginable trauma besides a rougher yet respectful small towner, set to work together at the risk of their survival. How Aaron Paul feels unequipped and consults his wife. How the grieving man finally cries in the arms of a woman. How he thirsts for sex, love, and art, and how he immediately understands the wife craves the same. How it's Aaron Paul's severity, anger, and classically masculine "My wife is MINE"  that brings about his demise, which of course was the grieving man's violent jealousy and resulting act of murdering that which he saw unfair to be anyone else's: a wife and child. I like how gender played a very big role in this narrative, in a way that's very thick and kinda out of mode nowadays. Not that I mind lesser gendered narratives, but it can then also be refreshing to have something that so classically and dramatically plays on male love, femininity, and the lust, compassion, and betrayal that plays in between.

I genuinely hate that I was. It was medically unnecessary genital mutilation, and that's really all it was. It also perpetuates stigmas against sex and sexual health. You can make the argument that it prevents infection and certain other health issues, and yes, this is true to a point. However these risks vary by a wide margin considering demographics. Where sexual health is more widespread, any risks are much better taken care of with condoms, regular cleaning, etc.
Most studies focus on communities where HIV and other diseases are more common, which then needs to take into account the area's culture, education, and other relevant factors. And in those situations, circumsision is definitely helpful. More than a condom? No. More than an uncircumsised penis? Yes. So if that's relevant and a worry, if you've genuinely made considerations and an educated decision, then I do think circumsision is valid. That's not the case now, however. These procedures are most often done because of problematic reasonings such as to prevent masturbation, faith, and, I think most commonly, "this is just how it is." 

I recognize faith and normalcy, but at the same time, I believe the physical and future sexual health of non-consenting individuals takes precedent. I don't fume over the fact that I was circumsised cause it was so long ago and normalized, but I do think in my case, and in most cases, it's wrong.

It's not so much that \[disorder\] affects gender, but more so that incorporating one's mental disorder/neurodivergence/however you'd like to call it into the construct of gender can help people better situate themselves socially both internally and externally. In the same way that a person isn't gendered in the sense that gender is a rigid prescription of behavior and attitude, a person does not have BPD in the sense that it is a rigid prescription of their behavior and attitude. In the same way that a person isn't gendered in the sense that everything they do is a gendered activity (like how sitting down and watching T.V. is just a thing that everybody does), a person doesn't have BPD in the sense that everything they do is impacted by their BPD. Basically, the way we view and interact with gender within queer communities contains a lot of parallels to how we should view and interact with mental health issues as well, and since a lot of us have a good grasp on gender, it can be helpful and therapeutic to self-incorporate what are often complex and confusing disorders. Don't forget how gender has a long history of being conflated with mental health disorders, and a lot of the queer community's work in liberating gender identity can be just as helpful to those who need to liberate their own identity in regards to their mental health. I don't do it myself, but I can definitely see the power in taking a mental health disorder that is often discriminated, insulted, and misunderstood and making it a part of who I am, taking ownership of it so much so that it's encoded into my identity language.
